Abel's Theorem

Does the sum of a series match the limit of its power series at 1?

If the series converges, the power series heads to the same value as x nears 1, as in the formula below. Even the divergent Grandi series points to one half in this limit. But that value is an Abel sum, a separate convention, not the sum.

For example, imagine a 🧑 friend shouting 1 and 0 in turns. If each shout is a bit quieter than the last, the running average settles near one half.

∑an→S ⇒ lim⁡x→1−∑anxn=S\sum a_n \to S \ \Rightarrow\ \lim_{x\to 1^{-}}\sum a_n x^n = S∑an​→S ⇒ x→1−lim​∑an​xn=S
∑n=0∞(−1)nxn=11+x→x→1−12\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^n x^n = \frac{1}{1+x} \xrightarrow[x\to 1^{-}]{} \frac{1}{2}n=0∑∞​(−1)nxn=1+x1​x→1−​21​

Prove the Abel sum of Grandi's series ∑n=0∞(−1)n\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} (-1)^n∑n=0∞​(−1)n is 12\frac{1}{2}21​.

Be explicit that the series itself diverges.

∑n=0N(−x)n=1−(−x)N+11+x→N→∞11+x(∣x∣<1)\sum_{n=0}^{N}(-x)^n = \frac{1-(-x)^{N+1}}{1+x} \xrightarrow[N\to\infty]{} \frac{1}{1+x} \quad (|x|<1)n=0∑N​(−x)n=1+x1−(−x)N+1​N→∞​1+x1​(∣x∣<1)
lim⁡x→1−11+x=12\lim_{x\to 1^{-}}\frac{1}{1+x} = \frac{1}{2}x→1−lim​1+x1​=21​
Show proof

  1. First, honestly: ∑n=0∞(−1)n\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} (-1)^n∑n=0∞​(−1)n diverges.

    The partial sums Sk=1S_k = 1Sk​=1 (kkk even), 000 (kkk odd) bounce forever with no limit (see the Grandi scene).

    What we compute now is not "the sum" of the series, but its Abel sum.

  2. For ∣x∣<1|x| < 1∣x∣<1 the geometric formula gives ∑n=0N(−x)n=1−(−x)N+11+x\sum_{n=0}^{N} (-x)^n = \frac{1-(-x)^{N+1}}{1+x}∑n=0N​(−x)n=1+x1−(−x)N+1​. E.g. at x=0.9x = 0.9x=0.9, N=20N = 20N=20: S20(0.9)=1−(−0.9)211.9≈0.5839S_{20}(0.9) = \frac{1-(-0.9)^{21}}{1.9} \approx 0.5839S20​(0.9)=1.91−(−0.9)21​≈0.5839, with exact error ∣(−0.9)21∣1.9≈0.0576\frac{|(-0.9)^{21}|}{1.9} \approx 0.05761.9∣(−0.9)21∣​≈0.0576.

  3. For ∣x∣<1|x| < 1∣x∣<1, (−x)N+1→0(-x)^{N+1} \to 0(−x)N+1→0, so letting N→∞N \to \inftyN→∞ gives ∑n=0∞(−1)nxn=11+x\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} (-1)^n x^n = \frac{1}{1+x}∑n=0∞​(−1)nxn=1+x1​. At x=0.9x = 0.9x=0.9 this is 1/1.9≈0.52631/1.9 \approx 0.52631/1.9≈0.5263 — the true target of the S20S_{20}S20​ above.

  4. Now let x→1−x \to 1^{-}x→1−: 11+x→12\frac{1}{1+x} \to \frac{1}{2}1+x1​→21​.

    Hence the Abel sum lim⁡x→1−∑n=0∞(−1)nxn=12\lim_{x \to 1^{-}} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} (-1)^n x^n = \frac{1}{2}limx→1−​∑n=0∞​(−1)nxn=21​.

    It coincides with the Cesàro sum 12\frac{1}{2}21​, but neither is "the sum" of a divergent series. ∎

Apply Abel's theorem to the alternating harmonic series ∑n=0∞(−1)nn+1=ln⁡2\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n}{n+1} = \ln 2∑n=0∞​n+1(−1)n​=ln2 to prove lim⁡x→1−∑n=0∞(−1)nxn+1n+1=ln⁡2\lim_{x \to 1^{-}} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n x^{n+1}}{n+1} = \ln 2limx→1−​∑n=0∞​n+1(−1)nxn+1​=ln2.

∑n=0N(−1)nxn+1n+1=ln⁡(1+x)−RN(x),∣RN(x)∣≤xN+2N+2\sum_{n=0}^{N}\frac{(-1)^n x^{n+1}}{n+1} = \ln(1+x) - R_N(x), \qquad |R_N(x)| \le \frac{x^{N+2}}{N+2}n=0∑N​n+1(−1)nxn+1​=ln(1+x)−RN​(x),∣RN​(x)∣≤N+2xN+2​
lim⁡x→1−ln⁡(1+x)=ln⁡2≈0.6931\lim_{x\to 1^{-}}\ln(1+x) = \ln 2 \approx 0.6931x→1−lim​ln(1+x)=ln2≈0.6931
Show proof

  1. Set an=(−1)nn+1a_n = \frac{(-1)^n}{n+1}an​=n+1(−1)n​. Then ∑n=0∞an\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n∑n=0∞​an​ converges by the Leibniz test (alternating, 1n+1↘0\frac{1}{n+1} \searrow 0n+11​↘0), and its value is ln⁡2≈0.6931\ln 2 \approx 0.6931ln2≈0.6931 (numerical check: at N=100000N = 100000N=100000 the partial sum is ≈0.69315218\approx 0.69315218≈0.69315218, error ≈5.0×10−6\approx 5.0 \times 10^{-6}≈5.0×10−6).

  2. Abel's theorem (Problem 1) gives lim⁡x→1−∑n=0∞anxn=ln⁡2\lim_{x \to 1^{-}} \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n x^n = \ln 2limx→1−​∑n=0∞​an​xn=ln2. But ∑n=0∞(−1)nxn+1n+1=x⋅∑n=0∞anxn\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^n x^{n+1}}{n+1} = x \cdot \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n x^n∑n=0∞​n+1(−1)nxn+1​=x⋅∑n=0∞​an​xn, and x→1x \to 1x→1, so the desired limit is 1⋅ln⁡2=ln⁡21 \cdot \ln 2 = \ln 21⋅ln2=ln2.

  3. A direct check agrees: restrict to 0≤x<10 \le x < 10≤x<1.

    Then ttt on the integration interval [0,x][0, x][0,x] satisfies 0≤t≤x<10 \le t \le x < 10≤t≤x<1 and 1+t≥11 + t \ge 11+t≥1.

    Integrating ∑n=0N(−t)n=1−(−t)N+11+t\sum_{n=0}^{N} (-t)^n = \frac{1-(-t)^{N+1}}{1+t}∑n=0N​(−t)n=1+t1−(−t)N+1​ (for ∣t∣<1|t| < 1∣t∣<1) from 000 to xxx gives ∑n=0N(−1)nxn+1n+1=ln⁡(1+x)−RN(x)\sum_{n=0}^{N} \frac{(-1)^n x^{n+1}}{n+1} = \ln(1+x) - R_N(x)∑n=0N​n+1(−1)nxn+1​=ln(1+x)−RN​(x) with ∣RN(x)∣≤∫0xtN+11+t dt≤∫0xtN+1 dt=xN+2N+2→0|R_N(x)| \le \int_0^x \frac{t^{N+1}}{1+t}\,dt \le \int_0^x t^{N+1}\,dt = \frac{x^{N+2}}{N+2} \to 0∣RN​(x)∣≤∫0x​1+ttN+1​dt≤∫0x​tN+1dt=N+2xN+2​→0 (N→∞N \to \inftyN→∞), using 1+t≥11 + t \ge 11+t≥1.

    So for 0≤x<10 \le x < 10≤x<1 the power series sums to exactly ln⁡(1+x)\ln(1+x)ln(1+x).

    The case x=1x = 1x=1 then follows by Abel's theorem (continuity), not by this integration step.

  4. Since ln⁡(1+x)→ln⁡2\ln(1+x) \to \ln 2ln(1+x)→ln2 (x→1−x \to 1^{-}x→1−), the limit is ln⁡2≈0.6931\ln 2 \approx 0.6931ln2≈0.6931 — matching Abel's theorem's prediction. This shows the Abel sum never contradicts the ordinary sum for a convergent series. ∎
